blocks.text: …complete relaxation
Definition and purpose 🐕
Off-leash following is the refinement of off-leash work. Together with our dog, we work towards reliably walking alongside each other over longer distances.

Off-leash following describes what used to be defined as heeling without a leash. In off-leash following, however, the emphasis is not on forced, close walking beside us, but rather on voluntary, motivated walking along in our vicinity – combined with reliable ways of controlling the dog when it is distracted by outside influences.

Off-leash following describes what used to be defined as heeling without a leash. In off-leash following, however, the emphasis is not on forced, close walking beside us, but rather on voluntary, motivated walking along in our vicinity – combined with reliable ways of controlling the dog when it is distracted by outside influences.
Prerequisites and training basics 📋

Correct work: What matters when training off-leash following is correct, trust-based work. For our dog to be able to implement off-leash following increasingly on a lasting basis, we must learn to master the interplay of motivation and corrective work and acquire perfect timing in applying it.
Training mood: Balanced, stress-free training is required.
Auxiliary line: For off-leash following training we need a light auxiliary line of max. 3–4 metres in length. Ideally made of light, sturdy webbing with a carabiner and a knot at the end.
Training environment and preparation 🌿

As with off-leash work, the training sessions initially take place without distraction in open terrain, far from hazardous environmental conditions. As training progresses, we apply the training with increasing distraction – but always only in situations and under conditions that allow a successful outcome.
Under no circumstances do we train off-leash following under dangerous conditions, near roads or similar high-risk environments. We prefer quiet paths; unstructured areas are less suitable.

The training takes place during relaxed walking, after our dog has been allowed to get rid of some of its excess energy through play and fun, and should be integrated into daily routines. In doing so, we make sure that bystanders are neither bothered nor endangered.
Step 1: Relaxed start with the auxiliary line 🚶
We walk at a calm pace, relaxed, with our dog on the training line. Through long-line training, it has already learned to walk together with us in the close range most of the time.

As soon as our dog is in a relaxed walking mode, we casually drop the training line without noticeably changing our walking rhythm. Everything should be very relaxed – we address our dog in a calm, praising voice with “Heel” and its name.
Step 2: Correction when leaving the close range 🔄
As long as our dog moves along beside us, everything is fine. If the distance between us and our dog increases significantly, we condition an interruption in our direction with a calm “Down”.

The goal is for our dog to learn to promptly take the down position when it leaves our close range. In this way, over time, we condition that we can protect our dog from dangers and from running off uncontrolled.
Through consistent application of this procedure, our dog is brought to trust our instruction and to carry it out without stress.
Step 3: Resuming walking ▶️

The dog now lies in front of us in “Down”. We let a few seconds pass for the situation to calm down and set off again together with the dog. To do this, we address our dog by name as relaxed and calm as possible. As a variation, we may set off with a small hand signal.
Our dog should then accompany us loosely again. This procedure is repeated throughout the entire off-leash following training.
Step 4: Praise and control in the close range 🌟

If the dog stays in the close range, everything is fine. At intervals, our dog can be calmly praised while walking along, verbally or by stroking. If the dog breaks away because of the praise, we bring it back into the down position.
It should learn that motivation of any kind should not lead to it leaving us.
Step 5: Transition to the free auxiliary line 🔓

As training progresses, we can move on to casually dropping the auxiliary line. Our dog should then continue to move along beside us within the desired close radius. Otherwise, we pick the line up again promptly but calmly and proceed as described above.

If, after a while of walking freely with the auxiliary line dropped, the dog lets itself be distracted and wants to move out of the trained area, we address it calmly and convincingly with “Down” and promptly pick up the auxiliary line. We immediately walk a few steps backwards and thereby support our dog in carrying out the required “Down” in our direction and learning to turn away from its original direction.
Step 6: Long-term transition to off-leash following 📈

This procedure with the dropped auxiliary line is trained over weeks until we are established to the point that the “Down” procedure works even under constantly growing distraction and our dog reliably stays beside us in the off-leash following area.

The transition from the dropped auxiliary line to off-leash following takes place over a training period of months, in which we constantly alternate between a held and a free-trailing line – depending on the environmental variables we are moving in. The phases in which we actively hold the auxiliary line should steadily decrease until we only walk with the auxiliary line dropped.

Little by little, the auxiliary line may then be shortened more and more, so that we approach the relaxed off-leash following state and can reliably secure our dog with “Down” in every situation in which it leaves off-leash following.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid tightening the auxiliary line during training.
Avoid switching too early to walking without an auxiliary line.
Avoid allowing the dog to leave the off-leash following radius through a delayed reaction.
Avoid stress during practice.
Avoid loud communication.
Under all circumstances, avoid failed attempts and break-out actions that are successful for the dog – i.e. running away.
Practical impulse: Months of consistency pay off

Off-leash following is the result of months of calm work. Every day, deliberately alternate between a held and a free-trailing auxiliary line – drop it as often as possible, but take hold of it consistently and calmly as soon as the dog wants to leave the radius. Calm praise while walking along strengthens the connection without motivating the dog to break away.
→ Do I enter off-leash following training in a focused and composed manner?
→ Was off-leash work trained for a few weeks as preparation?
→ Are we moving in clear and peaceful terrain?
→ Have I brought about a relaxed walking mode?
→ Am I confident in switching quickly and calmly between corrective and motivational work?
→ Do we drop the line as often as possible and give the dog the opportunity for off-leash following?
→ Do I carry out the correction procedure calmly?
→ Do I keep a calm pace and avoid running after the dog?
→ Am I ready, promptly and calmly, with the “Down” correction when the dog leaves the off-leash following radius?
→ After carrying out a correction, do I set off again calmly and composedly?
→ Do I give the whole training the necessary time and attention?
→ Do I heed the alternation between a held and a free-trailing line?
→ During off-leash following, do I praise verbally in a calm and composed way so as not to motivate the dog to break away?
→ Do I praise generously and affectionately at the end of the training procedure?
